flawed_step: Step 1 of the proof attempt: splitting a maximum flow into F unit s-t paths plus cycles, and claiming the arcs with positive flow number at least F+1. That needs at least one path to have length at least 2, meaning no unit of flow goes along a direct arc s→t. Nothing in the definitions rules out an arc s→t, so this step cannot be justified.
counterexample: Vertices {s, t, u, v}, with a single arc s→t of capacity 1; u and v are isolated. The maximum flow value is F = 1, since the cut {s} has capacity 1. The maximum flow f(s→t) = 1 gives positive flow to exactly 1 arc, which is F and not at least F+1.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A direct s→t arc carries one unit of flow using just one arc, so the claimed bound of F+1 arcs fails. In the smallest case, the only arc is s→t: F = 1, and the unique maximum flow gives positive flow to 1 arc.
